title: Rain if you like
hookLine: a herdsman and the Buddha, on the same riverbank, both tell the sky to rain
carry: my hut is open, my fire is out

cards: The weather app says heavy rain tonight. And there's a particular feeling, if you're lucky enough to have it: groceries in, laundry dry, windows shut, someone you love on the couch. Let it pour.
The second poem of the Sutta Nipata starts right there, with a cattle herder named Dhaniya on the bank of the Mahi river, the monsoon clouds rolling in.
He's done everything right, he's proud of it, and he sings it to the sky.

teach.h: MY RICE IS COOKED, MY HUT IS ROOFED
teach.b: Dhaniya's verse goes something like this. My rice is cooked, my cows are milked. I live with my people by the river.
My hut is roofed, my fire is lit. So rain if you like, sky. From nearby, another voice answers in the same rhythm.
It's the Buddha, who happens to be spending one night on the same riverbank. I'm free of anger, my stubbornness is gone. I stay one night by the river.
My hut is open, my fire is out. So rain if you like, sky. Hear the play on words?

teach.h: MY HUT IS OPEN, MY FIRE IS OUT
teach.b: Dhaniya's fire is the cooking fire; the Buddha's is the fire of craving, and it's gone out. Dhaniya's roof keeps the rain away; the Buddha's hut is open, nothing to protect. They trade verses.
Dhaniya: my cattle are strong, my wife is faithful, my sons are healthy. The Buddha: my raft is built, I've crossed the flood, I'm nobody's servant. Then the sky opens.

A great rain falls, and Dhaniya and his wife, the poem says, go for refuge and ask to go forth. Only then does Mara join in: whoever has children delights in children; whoever has cattle delights in cattle.

teach.h: GLAD OVER IT, GRIEVING OVER IT
teach.b: And the Buddha answers him: whoever has children grieves over children; whoever has cattle grieves over cattle.
What people have makes them glad and makes them worry, often in the same breath. And the poem never mocks Dhaniya. His security is real.
It just shows a second kind of shelter beside it.

how: Buddhist teachers often retell the Dhaniya poem to talk about two kinds of security, and in Theravada countries the rainy season is also when monks stay in one place for the three-month retreat.

o: the Buddha's name for the far shore
the herdsman safe and proud in his hut
a rain spirit called down by farmers

games.q: two men on one riverbank: tap the pairs.
p: those with children delight in them
those with children grieve over them

s: Dhaniya is a cattle herder by the Mahi river
he sings of his cooked rice, his milked cows and his roofed hut.
the poem mocks Dhaniya for caring about his home
it treats his security as real and sets a second kind of shelter beside it.
in the poem it's Mara who says possessions bring delight
the Buddha answers that the same things bring grief.

games.q: you're Dhaniya. the stranger on the riverbank has matched every verse you sang. now the rain comes down hard. what does the poem say happens next?
o: you chase him off your land.
you and your wife decide to go forth.
games.why: in the poem, as the great rain falls, Dhaniya and his wife take refuge and ask to go forth.

practice: Name, like Dhaniya, three shelters you have right now, a roof, a meal, a person, and let yourself be glad of them.
Then gently notice the worry that sits right next to each one, without fixing it: the gladness and the worry, holding hands. Let them both rest, and listen to the breath as if it were rain on a roof.

wordCard.voice: Dhaniya, the herdsman safe in his hut, and the Buddha free with an open one, both saying it to the same sky. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Dhaniya: the herdsman's name, from dhana, wealth: roughly, the wealthy one.

carryVoice: Your line: my hut is open, my fire is out. Two shelters under one sky. See you tomorrow.
